blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin storage and medication teaching
stem: A client asks how to store unopened insulin at home. Which instruction is most accurate?

options.A: Refrigerate unopened insulin at about 36°F to 46°F; if it freezes, let it thaw in the refrigerator and use it if the solution still looks normal and the package is sealed.
options.B: Refrigerate unopened insulin at about 36°F to 46°F; do not use insulin that has frozen, keep it away from heat and sunlight, and follow product-specific room-temperature limits.
options.C: Keep unopened insulin at 59°F to 86°F until the package expiration date; refrigeration is mainly needed after a vial or pen is opened, regardless of the specific product.
options.D: Refrigerate unopened insulin at about 36°F to 46°F; during temporary room-temperature storage, direct sunlight is acceptable if the surrounding temperature remains below 86°F.

rationale: Current FDA storage guidance states that insulin manufacturers recommend refrigeration at approximately 36°F to 46°F and that unopened insulin stored this way maintains potency until the package expiration date. FDA also directs users to avoid freezing, not use insulin that has been frozen, and keep insulin away from direct heat and direct sunlight. Because room-temperature allowances vary by insulin product and presentation, the specific product labeling should be followed. Therefore B is the best answer. A is unsafe because frozen insulin should not be used after thawing. C incorrectly treats room-temperature storage as valid through the package expiration date without regard to product-specific limits. D incorrectly permits direct sunlight exposure, which FDA advises avoiding.
educational_objective: Teach safe insulin storage: refrigerate unopened insulin at the recommended temperature when possible, do not use insulin that has been frozen, protect insulin from heat and sunlight, and follow product-specific room-temperature storage limits.
source_document_title: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
source_version_date: Current FDA web guidance; accessed 2026-08-26; no revision date displayed on the page
source_locator: Insulin Storage and Effectiveness > Insulin for Injection: manufacturers recommend refrigerator storage at approximately 36°F to 46°F; unopened insulin stored this way maintains potency until package expiration; avoid freezing and do not use insulin that has been frozen; keep insulin away from direct heat and direct sunlight. Product-specific labeling governs storage allowances outside refrigeration.
source_claim_supported: Unopened insulin should generally be refrigerated at approximately 36°F to 46°F; frozen insulin should not be used, heat and direct sunlight should be avoided, and room-temperature storage should follow product-specific labeling.
blueprint_locator: Printed p. 38, Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies: educate clients about medications; safely administer and handle medications; review pertinent medication data and evaluate medication-related risk.
candidate_reasons_resolved: Rewrote all four options as parallel storage instructions of comparable length.
Removed the obvious freezer/indefinite-storage/warm-window distractor pattern and retained one clearly source-supported best answer without a meaningful length cue.
audit_note: Clinical content was re-audited from zero after revision against current FDA storage guidance. B reflects the FDA-supported core storage principles while preserving product-specific room-temperature labeling. A wrongly allows use after freezing, C overgeneralizes room-temperature stability through package expiration, and D permits direct sunlight exposure. No second defensible answer or material cueing remains.
